reasons.reason: A CLI command runs in a terminal against a project's files; no page renders it and no browser loads it.

These commands write the configuration, catalogs, generated files and package metadata; they never reach the compiler, which is the only place a URL policy is read, and the configuration has no field for one.
XLIFF export and import read and write catalog files at build time; no page, browser or URL policy is involved.
The toolkit runs at build time in Node and is kept out of every browser graph; the focused consumer proves that absence.
An application runs one URL policy, so each policy row is exercised in its own column.

The request handler answers a request, on a server or in a test through the server seat: a build has no request for it to answer and fails on a declaration made while prerendering (spec 07 section 5), and a client navigation sends it no document request.
Server rendering configuration is read only by the server bundle; the browser bundle never imports it.
The server seat renders one response on the server platform and reads it; nothing renders or boots on a client.

These helpers run in a test host: TestBed, which Angular's unit-test builder starts on the browser platform before any setup file runs, creating components into a fixture, which is a client render. No reader reaches that page by a server render, a prerender, a hydration or a navigation after a document; the engines a test host runs in are the engine columns.
The entry point's helpers run in a test host or, in the server seat, answer one response and read it; nothing boots on a client after either, and nothing adopts markup a server drew.

A controllable participant, an in-memory loader map and the environment reset take no injector and read no platform: a test hands the first two to a localization it creates, and the reset clears the browser's address, cookies and storages. They run the same whatever renders the page, and the runtime they feed is claimed at render:client on its own rows.

A controllable participant, an in-memory loader map and the environment reset are handed no URL policy and read none: a participant is driven by the test, a loader by a catalog key, and the reset clears the address, cookies and storages whatever policy wrote them.

Equator produces the sitemap files as data, and the deployment writes or serves them to crawlers as they are (spec 07 section 11); no render of the application produces them and no page boots from them.
A caching declaration becomes a response header the server writes; no browser runs it, and a client navigation or hydration makes no document request.

A prerendered page has no response to carry a caching header; what the class does to a build is refuse a per-visitor or not-stored route and write no page for it (spec 07 section 9), which verify:consumer requires of the lazy route.

A renderer states what it decided with no page rendered at all (spec 07 section 5), so its answer is never a server-rendered page; verify:consumer claims both from the server's answers for the withdrawn and the unreachable dossier.

It describes the response a declaration produces. A build writes no page for a declared outcome (spec 07 section 5, checked by verify:consumer for the topic page), and a client navigation or a hydrated page has no response, which a release must not synthesize, so no build and no browser has a response for it to describe.

A route's sitemap entry is read only when the sitemap is projected (projectSitemap, spec 07 section 11), and the files that projection produces are served to crawlers as data; no render of a page reads it.

A page that declares its outcome while prerendering has no request to answer, so its render fails and no page is written (spec 07 section 5); verify:consumer lists the topic page for prerender with a value for each outcome and requires the refusal.
An alias is a second prefix a path-prefix policy accepts; the neutral and host policies have no prefix to alias.
Node 22 has no Intl.DurationFormat, so no duration can be formatted there; the exercise sheet holds Equator to the typed result spec 08 section 3 requires instead.

An outcome document is the head of an address answered with a status and no page of its own, and a prerendered file carries no status. A build writes files only for the routes its render table names, each by a route id checked against the projection; the not-found page is the wildcard, which is never prerendered, and a page that declares an absence or a removal while prerendering fails the build (spec 07 sections 5 and 9).

An address under an alias is answered with a correction before anything renders: the server draws no page and sends no application shell for it, a build writes none, and the page a browser adopts or renders afterwards is the address the correction names.

An address under a locale-neutral root is left to whatever serves it (spec 07 sections 3 and 4): Equator renders no page there, writes none, and has none for a browser to adopt or its router to draw, so what can be observed is the server declining it.

A build has no request, so no language preference reaches it, and the page it writes is adopted as it was decided; once hydrated only the stores are read again (spec 03 section 8), so the browser's languages never decide a prerendered page.
